title: The 'no waiter-flag' rule
body: Getting attention in a restaurant is by saying 'sumimasen' (excuse me) politely, not raising a hand or clicking. Many tables have a call-button; use it. Snapping fingers is rude.

title: Don't tip — it confuses staff
body: Tipping is not customary and often genuinely returned. Upscale restaurants may add a 10% service charge, which is not a tip — it's part of the menu price. See the Tipping page for context by venue.

title: Escalator sides
body: In Tokyo, stand on the LEFT, walk on the RIGHT. (Osaka is the opposite — left is for walkers.) Official campaigns now ask you to stand still and not walk, but the left-stand norm holds.

title: Blowing your nose in public
body: Considered rude. Sniff, or step away to a bathroom. Face masks while sick are normal and appreciated.

title: Chopsticks — what not to do
body: Never stand chopsticks upright in rice (funeral symbolism). Never pass food chopsticks-to-chopsticks (funeral ritual). Don't point with them. Rest them across the chopstick rest when not eating.

title: Onsen etiquette in 30 seconds
body: Wash thoroughly at the seated showers before entering the bath. No swimwear — bathing is nude. No photos, no phones. Long hair tied up, no dunking. Towels don't go in the water (rest on head). Cover visible tattoos with waterproof patches or pick a tattoo-friendly onsen.

title: Japanese toilets are a feature, not a chore
body: Washlet seats have heated seats, bidets, dryers, and white-noise buttons. Public restrooms are free, clean, and ubiquitous. Squat toilets still exist in older train stations — face the hooded end. No paid bathrooms; rare to find without paper.

title: Toilet slippers
body: In ryokan, homes, and some restaurants there are separate slippers at the toilet room entrance. Change into them when you enter, and — crucially — change back when you leave. Wearing toilet slippers into the dining room is a classic tourist flub.

title: Why are there no public bins?
body: Public trash cans largely disappeared after the 1995 sarin attacks. Carry your wrappers until you find a konbini bin, your hotel, or a station bin near the ticket gates. Separate trash into burnable / plastic / cans-bottles — signs show which is which.

title: Smoking is restricted — indoors and on some streets
body: Since 2020, most indoor public spaces are smoke-free. Streets in central wards (Chiyoda, Shinjuku, Shibuya, Minato) ban smoking outside designated areas; fines up to ¥2,000 apply. Look for 'designated smoking area' signs near stations.

title: Tax-free shopping basics
body: Visitors on a short-stay visa get 8-10% off at stores displaying the 'Japan. Tax-free Shop' logo, with a ¥5,500 minimum per store per day. Bring your passport to checkout. From 2026 the system moves to refund-at-departure — keep receipts and shopping bag seals intact.

title: Business hours are later than you think
body: Most shops open at 10:00 or 11:00 and close around 20:00-21:00. Department-store food halls (depachika) open 10:00, upstairs floors at 11:00. Restaurants commonly close 14:00-17:00 between lunch and dinner.

title: How Japanese addresses work
body: Addresses run from big to small: prefecture → ward → district → chōme (block) → banchi (lot) → go (building). Streets aren't named in most places — Google Maps is your friend. Taxi drivers appreciate a pin drop over a spoken address.

title: Last trains and priority seating
body: Trains stop 00:00-01:00 and resume around 04:45. Designated priority seats for elderly, pregnant, and disabled passengers are marked on the ends of each carriage — leave them open. Women-only cars run during rush hours on several lines (look for pink signs).

title: Carry photo ID at all times
body: Police occasionally request passports or residence cards. A photocopy is not enough — carry your passport. Losing it means a trip to your embassy, then to the Tokyo Immigration Bureau in Shinagawa.

title: Visa extensions
body: If you're on a short-stay visa and want to stay longer, visit the Tokyo Regional Immigration Services Bureau (5-5-30 Konan, Minato-ku). Some nationalities can extend once for another 90 days; paperwork and fees apply. Apply 1-2 weeks before your visa expires.

title: Kid-friendly Japan
body: Baby-change rooms in most department stores and large stations are spotless. Strollers are manageable but crowded trains and long station staircases are a challenge — baby carriers win. Konbini stock formula, diapers, and baby food.

title: Accessibility basics
body: Every Tokyo Metro and JR East station has step-free access to at least one exit. Staff at ticket gates will arrange portable ramps for trains — just show them your phone with the destination. Major attractions are broadly wheelchair-friendly; shrines and temples are hit-or-miss. Call ahead for restaurants — many still have step-up entrances.
